title: SSDD Problems
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton introduces Same Surface, Different Depth problems, sets of questions that look alike but need different mathematical ideas, and gives ten tips for using them. His case is that they are one of the best ways to bring interleaving into a lesson, since they trigger retrieval, force attention as topics switch, and make students identify deep structure instead of reacting to surface features. The tips are largely about managing the format: begin with an easy set, tell students they may start anywhere, make the top-left question the most accessible, and use the 4-2 solo-then-pair routine. He also suggests them as mixed-topic Do Nows, as repeated practice of high-value skills with small changes, and as GCSE revision. The piece is a compact, usable explanation of why the format works and how to introduce it.
points: SSDD sets work as interleaving in a box: retrieval of several ideas, attention that must keep switching, and discriminative contrast that forces students to read deep structure.
Because the format can look weird and impenetrable, the first set should be easy so students' first experience is a success.
Small teacher moves matter: say explicitly that students can start anywhere, and make the top-left question the most accessible since everyone starts there.
Asking a stuck student to write down which topic the question is on separates strategy-selection problems from procedure problems.
The format is flexible: four questions suit a Do Now, repeated sets with one changed number practise high-value skills, and one or two a week suit exam revision.
quotes: SSDD stands for Same Surface, Different Depth. They are a special set of problems that may look similar at first glance, but require different mathematical ideas to solve them.

SSDD Problems are one of the best ways I know of to tap into the power of interleaving. Interleaved practice involves mixing up the concepts involved instead of having students practice the same skills over and over.

Discriminative constant - this is the big one. Because each set of SSDD Problems has a surface feature in common (an image, a number, a context), students must think hard about how to identify the relevant deep structure so they can figure out what strategy to use to solve the problem.

This is particularly true in the case of SSDD Problems which can seem both weird and impenetrable, thus causing students to down tools before they have even started. Beginning with a relatively simple set of four questions should help students get used to the format, and build up the foundation of success needed for when the content demands increase.

Explicitly tell students that they can start on any question they like. This may be obvious to us, but countless times I have seen students spending all their time on the top-left question assuming they are not allowed to move on until they have completed it.

If students get really stuck on a question, ask them to write down what topic it is. This stops students from thinking that if they cannot answer the question then there is no point in them writing anything, and also gives you valuable insight as to whether strategy selection is the issue, or if the problem lies with carrying out a procedure.

SSDD Problems work really well as revision activities in the build-up to GCSE exams. Again, the benefits of retrieval, attention attenuation and discriminative contrast are exactly what is needed when taking on an unpredictable assessment.
